fetched_contents.text: Latent Syphilis Infants and children aged ≥1 month with diagnosed latent syphilis should be managed by a pediatric infectious disease specialist and receive a CSF examination. In addition, birth and maternal medical records should be reviewed to assess whether these infants and children have congenital or acquired syphilis. For those with congenital syphilis, treatment should be undertaken as described (see Congenital Syphilis). Those with acquired syphilis should be evaluated for sexual abuse (e.g., through consultation with child protection services) (see Sexual Assault or Abuse of Children). These regimens are for children who are not allergic to penicillin who have acquired syphilis and who have normal CSF examinations. Other Management Considerations All persons who have latent syphilis should be tested for HIV at the time of diagnosis or treatment. Those persons whose HIV test results are negative should be offered HIV PrEP. In geographic areas in which the prevalence of HIV infection is high or among populations vulnerable to HIV acquisition, persons who have early latent or late latent syphilis should be offered PrEP and retested for HIV in 3 months if the first HIV test result was negative. Persons who receive a diagnosis of latent syphilis and have neurologic or ocular signs and symptoms (e.g., cognitive dysfunction, motor or sensory deficits, ophthalmic or auditory symptoms, cranial nerve palsies, or symptoms or signs of meningitis or stroke) should be evaluated for neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis, or otosyphilis according to their clinical presentation (see Neurosyphilis, Ocular Syphilis, and Otosyphilis). If a person receives a delayed dose of penicillin in a course of weekly therapy for late latent syphilis or syphilis of unknown duration, the course of action that should be recommended is unclear. Clinical experience indicates that an interval of 10–14 days between doses of benzathine penicillin for latent syphilis might be acceptable before restarting the sequence of injections (i.e., if dose 1 is administered on day 0, dose 2 is administered on days 10–14). Pharmacologic considerations indicate that an interval of 7–9 days between doses, if feasible, might be preferred (610–612). Delayed doses are not optimal for pregnant women receiving therapy for latent syphilis (613). Pregnant women who have delays in any therapy dose >9 days between doses should repeat the full course of therapy. Follow-Up Quantitative nontreponemal serologic tests should be repeated at 6, 12, and 24 months. These serologic titers should be compared with the titer at the time of treatment. Persons with at least a fourfold sustained increase in nontreponemal test titer persisting for >2 weeks or who experienced signs or symptoms attributable to primary or secondary syphilis were likely reinfected or experienced treatment failure. These persons should be retreated and reevaluated for HIV infection. Among persons who have neurologic findings after a thorough neurologic examination or among persons with no neurologic findings and no sexual exposure during the previous year, a CSF examination is recommended. Treatment should be guided by CSF findings. Among persons with no neurologic findings after neurologic examination and who are sexually active, treatment with weekly injections of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM for 3 weeks is recommended. Optimal management of persons who have less than a fourfold decrease in titers 24 months after treatment (i.e., an inadequate serologic response) is unclear, especially if the initial titer was <1:8. At a minimum, these persons should receive additional clinical and serologic follow-up and be evaluated for HIV infection. If neurologic symptoms or signs are identified, a CSF evaluation is recommended, with the findings guiding management. If additional follow-up cannot be ensured or if an initially high titer (>1:32) does not decrease at least fourfold 24 months after treatment, retreatment with weekly injections of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM for 3 weeks is recommended. Because treatment failure might be the result of unrecognized CNS infection, CSF examination can be considered in such situations where follow-up is uncertain or initial high titers do not decrease after 24 months. If the CSF examination is negative, repeat treatment for latent syphilis is recommended. Serologic titers might not decrease despite a negative CSF examination and a repeated course of therapy, especially if the initial nontreponemal titer is low (<1:8); in these circumstances, the need for additional therapy or repeated CSF examinations is unclear but is usually not recommended. Serologic and clinical monitoring at least annually should continue to monitor for any sustained increases in nontreponemal titer. Management of Sex Partners See Syphilis, Management of Sex Partners. Special Considerations Penicillin Allergy The effectiveness of alternatives to penicillin in treating latent syphilis has not been well documented. Nonpregnant patients allergic to penicillin who have clearly defined early latent syphilis should respond to antibiotics recommended as alternatives to penicillin for treating primary and secondary syphilis (see Primary and Secondary Syphilis). The only acceptable alternatives for treating late latent syphilis or syphilis of unknown duration are doxycycline (100 mg orally 2 times/day) or tetracycline (500 mg orally 4 times/day), each for 28 days. The efficacy of these alternative regimens among persons with HIV infection has not been well studied. These therapies should be used only in conjunction with close serologic and clinical follow-up, especially among persons with HIV infection. fetched_contents.text: Syphilis is a systemic disease caused by T. pallidum. The disease has been divided into stages on the basis of clinical findings, which guide treatment and follow-up. Persons who have syphilis might seek treatment for signs or symptoms. Primary syphilis classically presents as a single painless ulcer or chancre at the site of infection but can also present with multiple, atypical, or painful lesions (564). Secondary syphilis manifestations can include skin rash, mucocutaneous lesions, and lymphadenopathy. Tertiary syphilis can present with cardiac involvement, gummatous lesions, tabes dorsalis, and general paresis. Latent infections (i.e., those lacking clinical manifestations) are detected by serologic testing. Latent syphilis acquired within the preceding year is referred to as early latent syphilis; all other cases of latent syphilis are classified as late latent syphilis or latent syphilis of unknown duration. T. pallidum can infect the CNS, which can occur at any stage of syphilis and result in neurosyphilis. Early neurologic clinical manifestations or syphilitic meningitis (e.g., cranial nerve dysfunction, meningitis, meningovascular syphilis, stroke, and acute altered mental status) are usually present within the first few months or years of infection. Late neurologic manifestations (e.g., tabes dorsalis and general paresis) occur 10 to >30 years after infection. Infection of the visual system (ocular syphilis) or auditory system (otosyphilis) can occur at any stage of syphilis but is commonly identified during the early stages and can present with or without additional CNS involvement. Ocular syphilis often presents as panuveitis but can involve structures in both the anterior and posterior segment of the eye, including conjunctivitis, anterior uveitis, posterior interstitial keratitis, optic neuropathy, and retinal vasculitis. Ocular syphilis can result in permanent vision loss. Otosyphilis typically presents with cochleo-vestibular symptoms, including tinnitus, vertigo, and sensorineural hearing loss. Hearing loss can be unilateral or bilateral, have a sudden onset, and progress rapidly. Otosyphilis can result in permanent hearing loss. Diagnostic Considerations Darkfield examinations and molecular tests for detecting T. pallidum directly from lesion exudate or tissue are the definitive methods for diagnosing early syphilis and congenital syphilis (565). Although no T. pallidum direct-detection molecular NAATs are commercially available, certain laboratories provide locally developed and validated PCR tests for detecting T. pallidum DNA. A presumptive diagnosis of syphilis requires use of two laboratory serologic tests: a nontreponemal test (i.e., Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or rapid plasma reagin [RPR] test) and a treponemal test (i.e., the T. pallidum passive particle agglutination [TP-PA] assay, various EIAs, chemiluminescence immunoassays [CIAs] and immunoblots, or rapid treponemal assays) (566–568). At least 18 treponemal-specific tests are cleared for use in the United States. Use of only one type of serologic test (nontreponemal or treponemal) is insufficient for diagnosis and can result in false-negative results among persons tested during primary syphilis and false-positive results among persons without syphilis or previously treated syphilis. Nontreponemal Tests and Traditional Algorithm False-positive nontreponemal test results can be associated with multiple medical conditions and factors unrelated to syphilis, including other infections (e.g., HIV), autoimmune conditions, vaccinations, injecting drug use, pregnancy, and older age (566,569). Therefore, persons with a reactive nontreponemal test should always receive a treponemal test to confirm the syphilis diagnosis (i.e., traditional algorithm). Nontreponemal test antibody titers might correlate with disease activity and are used for monitoring treatment response. Serum should be diluted to identify the highest titer, and results should be reported quantitatively. A fourfold change in titer, equivalent to a change of two dilutions (e.g., from 1:16 to 1:4 or from 1:8 to 1:32), is considered necessary for demonstrating a clinically significant difference between two nontreponemal test results obtained by using the same serologic test, preferably from the same manufacturer to avoid variation in results. Sequential serologic tests for a patient should be performed using the same testing method (VDRL or RPR), preferably by the same laboratory. VDRL and RPR are equally valid assays; however, quantitative results from the two tests cannot be compared directly with each other because the methods are different, and RPR titers frequently are slightly higher than VDRL titers. Nontreponemal test titers usually decrease after treatment and might become nonreactive with time. However, for certain persons, nontreponemal antibodies might decrease less than fourfold after treatment (i.e., inadequate serologic response) or might decline appropriately but fail to serorevert and persist for a long period. Atypical nontreponemal serologic test results (e.g., unusually high, unusually low, or fluctuating titers) might occur regardless of HIV status. When serologic tests do not correspond with clinical findings indicative of primary, secondary, or latent syphilis, presumptive treatment is recommended for persons with risk factors for syphilis, and use of other tests (e.g., biopsy for histology and immunostaining and PCR of lesion) should be considered. For the majority of persons with HIV infection, serologic tests are accurate and reliable for diagnosing syphilis and evaluating response to treatment. fetched_contents.text: Syphilis: Treatment and monitoring INTRODUCTION Syphilis is an infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum. During the initial phase of infection, the organism disseminates widely, setting the stage for subsequent manifestations. If untreated, syphilis can have a number of significant late adverse outcomes including cardiovascular, gummatous, and neurologic complications. The management of syphilis is based upon its classification into stages of disease: early syphilis (includes primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis); late (includes late latent, cardiovascular, and gummatous syphilis); and neurosyphilis (includes central nervous system disease and ocular syphilis at any time). A patient should understand that latent syphilis is a stage of infection without visible symptoms, and it is classified based on the time since infection. Early latent syphilis is acquired within the preceding year, while late latent syphilis or latent syphilis of unknown duration refers to cases acquired more than one year ago or where the exact duration is unclear [N1-F1]. This distinction matters because treatment recommendations and monitoring plans differ by stage. The CDC explicitly separates early latent syphilis from late latent syphilis in its guidelines, with late latent syphilis having different treatment options and follow-up expectations [N1-F1].

Diagnosis of latent syphilis relies on serologic testing, not visible lesions. The CDC says that syphilis is detected by serologic testing, and a presumptive diagnosis requires two laboratory serologic tests: a nontreponemal test (such as RPR or VDRL) and a treponemal test (such as TP-PA, EIAs, CIAs, immunoblots, or rapid treponemal assays) [N2-F2]. The CDC also notes that a reactive nontreponemal test should always be followed by a treponemal test to confirm the diagnosis, because using only one type of serologic test can lead to false-negative or false-positive results [N2-F2]. This means latent syphilis is diagnosed by lab tests rather than by symptoms alone.

When latent syphilis is treated versus monitored depends on whether the infection is early or late, and whether there are signs of neurosyphilis or other complicating features. The CDC says that persons with latent syphilis should be tested for HIV at diagnosis and offered HIV PrEP in some settings [N1-F1]. For persons without neurologic findings, the CDC recommends weekly injections of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM for 3 weeks [N1-F1]. If neurologic findings are present, a CSF examination is recommended, and treatment should be guided by CSF findings [N1-F1]. This shows that latent syphilis is treated when the infection is active or when there is evidence of neurosyphilis, while monitoring is part of follow-up after treatment rather than a substitute for treatment itself [N1-F1]. The CDC also emphasizes that follow-up serology is repeated at 6, 12, and 24 months after treatment, and that serologic titers should be compared with the titer at treatment to guide further action [N2-R1].

Overall, a patient should know that latent syphilis is diagnosed by serologic tests, classified into early or late latent based on duration, and treated when active disease or neurosyphilis is present, with monitoring focused on post-treatment response and complications [N1-F1][N2-F2][N2-R1].

Follow-up actions beyond lab testing are essential because syphilis is highly contagious and can spread even when people are asymptomatic. The Canadian guideline states that case finding and partner notification are critical to controlling syphilis, and all sexual or other contacts should be notified, clinically evaluated, and tested [N4-R1]. This means that after diagnosis, patients should expect their provider to notify sexual partners and arrange testing for those contacts.

Repeat screening for the patient over time is also important. The CDC recommends quantitative nontreponemal serologic tests be repeated at 6, 12, and 24 months after treatment, and it says that repeat screening can be considered in other clinical situations including inconclusive serology and ongoing risk [N2-F2][N4-R4]. The CDC also notes that after treatment of early or late latent syphilis, quantitative nontreponemal titers should be measured at 6, 12, and 24 months [N5-F3]. These repeated tests are not optional; they are part of the monitoring plan to detect treatment failure, reinfection, or incomplete response.

Instructions for avoiding reinfection should be practical and specific. The CDC says that people who are treated with alternative treatments may take longer to become non-infectious, and that contacts with lesions suspected of being syphilis should have a lesion swab [N3-R5]. The Canadian guideline also emphasizes that after infection, people are no longer infectious to sexual partners after 2 years if the infection is late latent syphilis, but it does not change the need for partner notification and screening [N4-R2]. This suggests that patients should avoid sexual activity until their provider confirms that they are no longer infectious, and they should use condoms or other barrier methods if they are sexually active during follow-up. The CDC also says that persons who receive a delayed dose of penicillin in a course of weekly therapy for late latent syphilis or syphilis of unknown duration may need a longer interval before restarting therapy, and that pregnant women with delays should repeat the full course of therapy [N1-F1]. This highlights the importance of completing treatment as prescribed and not resuming therapy too soon.

In summary, follow-up actions beyond lab testing include partner notification and contact screening, repeat screening for the patient over time, and instructions to avoid reinfection through safer sexual practices and completion of prescribed therapy [N4-R1][N2-F2][N4-R2][N3-R5].

After treatment for latent syphilis, the recommended repeat serology intervals are 6, 12, and 24 months [N2-R1]. The CDC explicitly states that quantitative nontreponemal serologic tests should be repeated at these intervals and that serologic titers should be compared with the titer at the time of treatment [N2-R1]. The CDC also says that for syphilis follow-up, CDC recommends a quantitative NTT for monitoring the serological response to treatment, and that TT titers do not correlate with disease activity [N2-R3]. This means that follow-up testing is not meant to diagnose active infection, but rather to monitor treatment response.

What test results mean at each follow-up visit depends on how the titer changes. The CDC notes that persons with at least a fourfold sustained increase in nontreponemal test titer persisting for >2 weeks or who experienced signs or symptoms attributable to primary or secondary syphilis were likely reinfected or experienced treatment failure [N1-F1]. It also says that persons with no neurologic findings and no sexual exposure during the previous year should be treated with weekly injections of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM for 3 weeks [N1-F1]. If additional follow-up cannot be ensured or if an initially high titer (>1:32) does not decrease at least fourfold 24 months after treatment, retreatment with weekly injections of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM for 3 weeks is recommended [N1-F1]. The CDC also emphasizes that serologic and clinical monitoring at least annually should continue to monitor for any sustained increases in nontreponemal titer [N1-F1].

When to repeat testing if treatment is repeated depends on whether the patient has had a prior course and the reason for the repeat. The CDC says that if a person receives a delayed dose of penicillin in a course of weekly therapy for late latent syphilis or syphilis of unknown duration, the course of action that should be recommended is unclear, and that clinical experience suggests an interval of 10–14 days between doses might be acceptable before restarting the sequence, but 7–9 days is preferred if feasible [N1-F1]. For pregnant women, delays >9 days between doses should trigger a full course of therapy [N1-F1]. This means that if treatment is repeated, the provider should monitor closely and may adjust the timing or reinstitute the full regimen depending on how the prior course was interrupted.

In short, after latent syphilis treatment, patients should have repeat serology at 6, 12, and 24 months, with results interpreted in terms of titer change, signs of reinfection or treatment failure, and whether retreatment is needed. If treatment is repeated, close follow-up is especially important, and the CDC does not provide a fixed rule for every case, so patients should follow their provider’s guidance [N2-R1][N2-R3][N1-F1].

# Integrated patient-facing follow-up plan for latent syphilis

## 1) What latent syphilis is and why follow-up matters
Latent syphilis is a stage of syphilis infection when a person has no visible symptoms, but the infection is still active and can be passed on to others [N1-F1]. It is classified into two main groups:  
- **Early latent syphilis** is acquired within the preceding year, and  
- **Late latent syphilis** or latent syphilis of unknown duration refers to cases acquired more than one year ago or where the exact duration is unclear [N1-F1].  

Because latent syphilis is asymptomatic, diagnosis cannot be made by symptoms alone. Instead, it is diagnosed by serologic testing. A presumptive diagnosis requires two laboratory serologic tests: a nontreponemal test (such as RPR or VDRL) and a treponemal test (such as TP-PA, EIAs, CIAs, immunoblots, or rapid treponemal assays) [N2-F2]. A reactive nontreponemal test should always be followed by a treponemal test to confirm the diagnosis, because using only one type of serologic test can lead to false-negative or false-positive results [N2-F2].

Follow-up matters because latent syphilis can still cause complications and reinfection is possible. The CDC emphasizes that persons with latent syphilis should be tested for HIV at diagnosis and offered HIV PrEP in some settings [N1-F1]. If neurologic findings are present, a CSF examination is recommended, and treatment should be guided by CSF findings [N1-F1]. That means follow-up is not just about lab tests; it is about monitoring for treatment response, complications, and whether the infection has been fully cleared.

## 2) When latent syphilis is treated versus when it is monitored
Latent syphilis is treated when the infection is active or when there are signs of neurosyphilis or other complicating features. The CDC recommends weekly injections of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM for 3 weeks for persons with no neurologic findings and no recent sexual exposure [N1-F1]. If neurologic findings are present, treatment should be guided by CSF findings [N1-F1]. For late latent syphilis or syphilis of unknown duration, the CDC says that doxycycline (100 mg orally 2 times/day) or tetracycline (500 mg orally 4 times/day) may be used, but these alternatives should be used only in conjunction with close serologic and clinical follow-up, especially among persons with HIV infection [N1-F1].

In contrast, monitoring is part of the follow-up after treatment. Monitoring includes repeat serology and clinical evaluation to detect treatment failure, reinfection, or incomplete response. The CDC says that quantitative nontreponemal serologic tests should be repeated at 6, 12, and 24 months after treatment [N2-R1], and that serologic and clinical monitoring at least annually should continue [N1-F1]. This means that latent syphilis is treated when active disease or neurosyphilis is present, and monitored when the infection is in remission or after treatment has been completed [N1-F1][N2-R1].

## 3) What follow-up testing should be planned after treatment
After treatment, the recommended repeat serology intervals are **6, 12, and 24 months** [N2-R1]. The CDC explicitly states that quantitative nontreponemal serologic tests should be repeated at these intervals and that serologic titers should be compared with the titer at the time of treatment [N2-R1]. The CDC also says that for syphilis follow-up, CDC recommends a quantitative NTT for monitoring the serological response to treatment, and that TT titers do not correlate with disease activity [N2-R3]. So the purpose of these tests is not to prove reinfection, but to show whether the infection is responding to treatment or whether there is a new problem.

At each follow-up visit, test results are interpreted in terms of titer change. The CDC notes that persons with at least a fourfold sustained increase in nontreponemal test titer persisting for >2 weeks or who experienced signs or symptoms attributable to primary or secondary syphilis were likely reinfected or experienced treatment failure [N1-F1]. In such cases, persons should be retreated and reevaluated for HIV infection [N1-F1]. If additional follow-up cannot be ensured or if an initially high titer (>1:32) does not decrease at least fourfold 24 months after treatment, retreatment with weekly injections of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM for 3 weeks is recommended [N1-F1]. The CDC also says that serologic and clinical monitoring at least annually should continue to monitor for any sustained increases in nontreponemal titer [N1-F1].

If treatment is repeated, the timing of repeat testing should be guided by how the prior course was interrupted. The CDC says that if a person receives a delayed dose of penicillin in a course of weekly therapy for late latent syphilis or syphilis of unknown duration, the course of action is unclear, and clinical experience suggests an interval of 10–14 days between doses might be acceptable before restarting the sequence, but 7–9 days is preferred if feasible [N1-F1]. For pregnant women, delays >9 days between doses should trigger a full course of therapy [N1-F1]. That means repeat testing after a repeated course is not a fixed schedule; it depends on how the treatment was completed and how the provider interprets the prior response.

## 4) Follow-up actions beyond lab testing
Syphilis is highly contagious, and follow-up goes beyond blood tests because the infection can spread even when people are asymptomatic. The Canadian guideline states that **case finding and partner notification are critical to controlling syphilis**, and all sexual or other contacts should be notified, clinically evaluated, and tested [N4-R1]. This means that after diagnosis, patients should expect their provider to notify sexual partners and arrange testing for those contacts.

Repeat screening for the patient over time is also important. The CDC recommends quantitative nontreponemal serologic tests be repeated at 6, 12, and 24 months after treatment, and it says repeat screening can be considered in other clinical situations including inconclusive serology and ongoing risk [N2-F2][N4-R4]. The CDC also says that after treatment of early or late latent syphilis, quantitative nontreponemal titers should be measured at 6, 12, and 24 months [N5-F3]. These repeated tests are part of the monitoring plan to detect treatment failure, reinfection, or incomplete response.

Instructions for avoiding reinfection should be practical and specific. The CDC says that people who are treated with alternative treatments may take longer to become non-infectious, and that contacts with lesions suspected of being syphilis should have a lesion swab [N3-R5]. The Canadian guideline also emphasizes that after infection, people are no longer infectious to sexual partners after 2 years if the infection is late latent syphilis, but it does not change the need for partner notification and screening [N4-R2]. That suggests patients should avoid sexual activity until their provider confirms that they are no longer infectious and should use condoms or other barrier methods if they are sexually active during follow-up.

## 5) How duration and treatment history affect long-term monitoring
Duration and treatment history affect long-term monitoring because latent syphilis is classified as early or late, and treatment duration varies accordingly. The CDC says that treatment for late latent syphilis (>1 years’ duration) and tertiary syphilis requires a longer duration of therapy because organisms are more persistent [N5-R1]. The CDC also says that late latent syphilis is infection for more than 2 years in the absence of any symptoms, and that after 2 years people are no longer infectious to sexual partners [N4-R2]. However, the CDC does not say that 2 years automatically means the infection is cured, only that people are no longer infectious to sexual partners after 2 years [N4-R2]. That means monitoring is still needed even after the infectious period has passed.

If reinfection or treatment failure is suspected, the CDC recommends a different course of action. A fourfold sustained increase in nontreponemal test titer persisting for >2 weeks or signs/symptoms attributable to primary or secondary syphilis suggest reinfection or treatment failure [N1-F1]. In such cases, persons should be retreated and reevaluated for HIV infection [N1-F1]. If neurologic findings are present, a CSF examination is recommended, and treatment should be guided by CSF findings [N1-F1]. If additional follow-up cannot be ensured or if an initially high titer (>1:32) does not decrease at least fourfold 24 months after treatment, retreatment with weekly injections of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM for 3 weeks is recommended [N1-F1]. The CDC also says that persons with no neurologic findings after a thorough neurologic examination and who are sexually active should be treated with weekly injections of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM for 3 weeks [N1-F1].

How long to monitor after a single course of treatment is also important. The CDC recommends serologic and clinical monitoring at least annually after treatment [N1-F1]. It also says that quantitative nontreponemal serologic tests should be repeated at 6, 12, and 24 months [N2-R1]. The CDC further notes that if the CSF examination is negative, repeat treatment for latent syphilis is recommended [N1-F1]. The UpToDate source confirms that treatment and monitoring after treatment will be reviewed, and that monitoring is part of the care plan [N5-F3]. So patients should expect ongoing follow-up, not just one-time testing.

## 6) Patient-friendly summary of the follow-up plan
If you have latent syphilis, your follow-up plan should include these steps:

1. **Diagnosis and classification:**  
   - Latent syphilis is diagnosed by blood tests, not by symptoms [N2-F2].  
   - It is classified as early latent syphilis if acquired within the preceding year, or late latent syphilis if acquired more than one year ago or where the exact duration is unclear [N1-F1].  
   - Treatment is guided by whether the infection is active or whether there are signs of neurosyphilis [N1-F1].

2. **Treatment:**  
   - Early latent syphilis is usually treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly for 3 weeks [N1-F1].  
   - Late latent syphilis or syphilis of unknown duration may be treated with doxycycline (100 mg orally 2 times/day) or tetracycline (500 mg orally 4 times/day), but these alternatives should be used with close follow-up [N1-F1].  
   - If neurologic findings are present, treatment should be guided by CSF findings [N1-F1].

3. **Follow-up testing after treatment:**  
   - Repeat serology should be done at **6, 12, and 24 months** after treatment [N2-R1].  
   - Results are interpreted by comparing titers with the titer at the time of treatment [N2-R1].  
   - If there is a fourfold sustained increase in titer or signs/symptoms of reinfection, retreatment is recommended and HIV reevaluation is needed [N1-F1].  
   - If the titer does not decrease fourfold 24 months after treatment, retreatment is also recommended [N1-F1].  
   - If treatment is repeated, close follow-up is important and the timing of repeat testing should be guided by how the prior course was completed [N1-F1].

4. **Actions beyond lab testing:**  
   - Notify sexual partners and arrange testing for contacts [N4-R1].  
   - Repeat screening for the patient over time, especially if serology is inconclusive or risk remains [N2-F2][N4-R4].  
   - Avoid sexual activity until your provider confirms that you are no longer infectious, and use condoms or other barrier methods during follow-up [N3-R5][N4-R2].  
   - Complete prescribed therapy as directed and do not restart treatment too soon, especially if there was a delay [N1-F1].

5. **Long-term monitoring:**  
   - Monitor at least annually after treatment [N1-F1].  
   - If reinfection or treatment failure is suspected, retreatment and reevaluation are recommended [N1-F1].  
   - If the infection has been treated for more than 2 years, people are no longer infectious to sexual partners, but monitoring continues because the infection may not be completely cleared [N4-R2][N1-F1].  

## 7) Bottom line
Your follow-up plan for latent syphilis is designed to ensure the infection is fully treated, to detect any treatment failure or reinfection, and to protect your sexual partners. It includes:  
- Blood tests at 6, 12, and 24 months after treatment [N2-R1],  
- Partner notification and contact screening [N4-R1],  
- Annual monitoring after treatment [N1-F1], and  
- Close follow-up if treatment is repeated or if results suggest reinfection or failure [N1-F1].  

This plan is not optional — it is part of the standard care for latent syphilis and is intended to help keep you healthy and prevent transmission to others [N1-F1][N2-R1][N4-R1].

A reactive nontreponemal test should always be followed by a treponemal test to confirm the diagnosis, because using only one type of serologic test can lead to false-negative or false-positive results [N2-F2].

The CDC emphasizes that persons with latent syphilis should be tested for HIV at diagnosis and offered HIV PrEP in some settings [N1-F1]. If neurologic findings are present, a CSF examination is recommended, and treatment should be guided by CSF findings [N1-F1]. ## 6) Patient-friendly summary of the follow-up plan
If you have latent syphilis, your follow-up plan should include these steps:

1. **Diagnosis and classification:**  
   - Latent syphilis is diagnosed by blood tests, not by symptoms [N2-F2].  
   - It is classified as early latent syphilis if acquired within the preceding year, or late latent syphilis if acquired more than one year ago or where the exact duration is unclear [N1-F1].

- Blood tests at 6, 12, and 24 months after treatment [N2-R1],  
- Partner notification and contact screening [N4-R1],  
- Annual monitoring after treatment [N1-F1], and

Latent syphilis is a stage of syphilis infection when a person has no visible symptoms, but the infection is still active and can be passed on to others [N1-F1]. It is classified into two main groups:  
- **Early latent syphilis** is acquired within the preceding year, and  
- **Late latent syphilis** or latent syphilis of unknown duration refers to cases acquired more than one year ago or where the exact duration is unclear [N1-F1].  

Because latent syphilis is asymptomatic, diagnosis cannot be made by symptoms alone. Instead, it is diagnosed by serologic testing. Latent syphilis is treated when the infection is active or when there are signs of neurosyphilis or other complicating features. The CDC says that quantitative nontreponemal serologic tests should be repeated at 6, 12, and 24 months after treatment [N2-R1], and that serologic and clinical monitoring at least annually should continue [N1-F1].
